meta.title: Current liabilities, provisions and contingencies
meta.summary: Accounts and notes payable, current maturities and refinancing, unearned revenue and gift cards, sales taxes and payroll, loss and gain contingencies, assurance warranties, and asset retirement obligations.

videos.title: Payables and notes
videos.take: Current liabilities are obligations expected to be settled within a year or the operating cycle; accrue interest on notes

scenes.say: Bluestem owes money to suppliers, banks, employees, customers and governments. Most of it is due within the year.

sub: Expected to be settled from current assets
or new current liabilities, within a year
scenes.say: A current liability is an obligation whose settlement is expected to use current assets or create other current liabilities, within one year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer.

scenes.heading: Common current liabilities
scenes.say: Common examples: accounts payable, short-term notes payable, the current portion of long-term debt, dividends declared but unpaid, unearned revenues and customer deposits, and taxes and payroll liabilities.

scenes.heading: Interest-bearing note, signed November 1
scenes.say: On November 1, Bluestem signs a $120,000, six-month, eight percent note with its bank to fund winter production. By December 31, two months of interest, $1,600, has accrued. At maturity on May 1, Bluestem will owe $124,800.

scenes.heading: December 31 accrual
scenes.say: The year-end entry accrues $1,600 of interest expense and interest payable. A zero-interest-bearing note would instead be recorded at its present value, with the discount amortized as interest.

scenes.q: A $90,000, 10%, 4-month note was signed December 1. Accrued interest at December 31?
scenes.say: Quick check. A ninety thousand dollar, ten percent, four-month note was signed December 1. Accrued interest at December 31? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Refinancing, deposits and gift cards
videos.take: Debt refinanced before the statements are issued can be long-term; unearned revenue is a liability until earned

scenes.say: Bluestem has a $500,000 note due in March. It plans to roll it into a five-year loan. Current or long-term?

scenes.big: Short-term debt expected to be refinanced
sub: Long-term only if refinanced, or a firm
scenes.say: Short-term debt can be classified as long-term only if the company intends to refinance it and actually does, or signs a firm, noncancelable financing agreement, before the financial statements are issued. Intent alone isn't enough.
Bluestem signs the five-year loan on February 10, before its statements are issued on March 1. The $500,000 is reported as long-term at December 31.

scenes.heading: Gift cards sold in December
scenes.say: Bluestem's stores sold $50,000 of gift cards in December; customers redeemed $30,000 by year-end. The other $20,000 is unearned revenue, a liability, until the cards are used.
Some cards are never used. If Bluestem can estimate this breakage, it recognizes the expected unredeemed amount as revenue in proportion to the pattern of redemptions.

scenes.q: Bluestem intends to refinance a note due in April but has no signed agreement when the statements are issued. The note is:
scenes.say: Quick check. Bluestem intends to refinance a note due in April but has no signed agreement when the statements are issued. How is the note classified? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's A, current. Intent alone isn't enough.

videos.title: Sales taxes and payroll
videos.take: Taxes collected for governments are liabilities; payroll has withholdings and employer taxes

scenes.say: Bluestem collects money it doesn't own: sales taxes and amounts withheld from paychecks.

scenes.heading: Sales tax included in receipts
scenes.say: A Bluestem store rang up $21,200, including six percent sales tax. Sales are twenty-one two divided by one point oh six, $20,000, and sales tax payable is $1,200. Sales tax is never revenue.

scenes.heading: Weekly payroll
scenes.say: Weekly gross wages are $100,000. Bluestem withholds seven point six five percent for Social Security and Medicare, $7,650, and $15,000 of federal income tax. Employees receive $77,350.

scenes.heading: Employer payroll taxes
scenes.say: Bluestem also owes its own payroll taxes: a matching $7,650 of FICA and $2,000 of unemployment taxes. Payroll tax expense is $9,650 on top of wages.
Vacation pay is accrued as employees earn it, if the rights vest or accumulate and the amount can be estimated. Sick pay that doesn't vest may be expensed when taken.

scenes.q: Receipts of $53,500 include 7% sales tax. Sales tax payable?
scenes.say: Quick check. Receipts of fifty-three thousand five hundred include seven percent sales tax. Sales tax payable? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Contingencies
videos.take: Accrue probable, estimable losses; disclose reasonably possible ones; never recognize gain contingencies

scenes.say: A customer whose Bluestem kayak capsized has sued for $1 million.

scenes.heading: Loss contingencies
scenes.say: A loss contingency is accrued if a loss is probable and can be reasonably estimated. If it's reasonably possible, or probable but not estimable, it's disclosed in the notes. If remote, nothing is required.

scenes.heading: The capsize lawsuit
rows: No amount in range better than others
scenes.say: Bluestem's lawyers say a loss is probable, somewhere between $200,000 and $500,000, with no amount more likely than another. GAAP requires accruing the minimum, $200,000, and disclosing the range. If one amount were more likely, Bluestem would accrue that.

scenes.heading: Recording the loss
scenes.say: Debit Litigation Loss and credit Litigation Liability for $200,000. The notes describe the case and the possible additional $300,000.
Gain contingencies, like Bluestem's own patent suit against a copycat, aren't recognized until realized. They may be disclosed, carefully, to avoid misleading users.

scenes.q: A loss is reasonably possible and estimated at $80,000. Treatment?
scenes.say: Quick check. A loss is reasonably possible and estimated at eighty thousand. Treatment? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Assurance-type warranties
videos.take: Estimate warranty costs when the product is sold; actual repairs reduce the liability

scenes.say: Every Bluestem kayak carries a two-year warranty against defects.

sub: Promises the product works as described:
scenes.say: An assurance-type warranty promises the product meets agreed specifications. It's not a separate service, so the expected cost is accrued as an expense when the kayaks are sold.

scenes.heading: 2028 warranty estimate
scenes.say: Bluestem sold 4,000 kayaks and expects warranty costs of $25 each: $100,000 of warranty expense in 2028. Repairs during the year cost $30,000, leaving a $70,000 liability.

scenes.heading: The entries
scenes.say: Accrue the $100,000 expense and liability. As repairs are made, reduce the liability and credit the cash, parts and labor used.
An extended warranty that customers can buy separately is a service-type warranty: a separate performance obligation whose revenue is deferred. You'll see it in the revenue lectures.

scenes.q: Sales 2,000 units; expected warranty cost $30 per unit; repairs this year $18,000. Year-end liability?
scenes.say: Quick check. Two thousand units sold; expected warranty cost thirty dollars a unit; repairs this year eighteen thousand. Year-end liability? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Asset retirement obligations
videos.take: Record the present value of legal retirement costs as a liability and add it to the asset

scenes.say: Bluestem's lease on its paint shop requires it to remove underground solvent tanks when it leaves in ten years.

sub: A legal obligation to retire a
long-lived asset: recorded at fair value
scenes.say: An asset retirement obligation is a legal obligation tied to retiring a long-lived asset. It's recorded at fair value, usually the present value of expected costs, when incurred.

scenes.heading: Measuring the obligation
scenes.say: Removal is expected to cost $80,000 in ten years. Discounted at Bluestem's six percent credit-adjusted risk-free rate, the obligation is $44,671.

scenes.heading: Recording the ARO
scenes.say: Bluestem adds $44,671 to the cost of the asset and records the liability. The asset cost is depreciated over ten years, $4,467 a year.

scenes.heading: Year 1 expenses
scenes.say: Each year, the liability grows by accretion expense, six percent of its balance: $2,680 in year one. By year ten it reaches $80,000. Total year-one cost: $7,147.

scenes.q: ARO recorded at $50,000; credit-adjusted rate 8%. Year-1 accretion expense?
scenes.say: Quick check. An ARO is recorded at fifty thousand; credit-adjusted rate eight percent. Year-one accretion expense? Pause and pick.

case: The capsize lawsuit and the covenant

Bluestem's loan covenant limits total liabilities to 60% of total assets. Before year-end entries: liabilities $2,700,000; assets $4,600,000. Pending items: the capsize lawsuit (probable, $200,000–$500,000, no best estimate); a reasonably possible $300,000 environmental fine; and an expected $120,000 refund from a customs dispute Bluestem is likely to win. The founder suggests disclosing the lawsuit only, and recording the customs refund.
Compute the ratio before and after correct accounting.

Before 58.7%. After accrual of 200,000 (loss reduces equity, assets unchanged): 2,900,000 ÷ 4,600,000 = 63.0%: covenant breached. Lawsuit must be accrued at the minimum; customs refund is a gain contingency, not recognized. Disclose range for lawsuit, fine (reasonably possible), possibly the refund. Ethics: pressure to misstate; talk to lender for waiver.
exam: Explain the criteria for accruing a loss contingency and how ranges are handled.
Probable and reasonably estimable; best estimate in range, else minimum; disclose nature and range; reasonably possible disclose; remote none; gains not recognized.
Bluestem must remove tanks in 10 years at an expected cost of $80,000; credit-adjusted rate 6% (factor 0.55839). Record the ARO and year-1 entries.
